title: Mark (25 April)
hook: the evangelist behind the Gospel that starts with a voice in the desert; his symbol is the lion

segments.voice: Yesterday, George, the soldier under the dragon legend. Your line was slay the dragon. What was your first small move? Day nine hundred eighty-four.

No manger. No angels. No family tree. One sentence of title, and then a shout from the wilderness. That's how the Gospel of Mark begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." A few lines later, a voice crying in the desert, John the Baptist in camel's hair, and Jesus already walking down to the river. Some readers call it the Gospel in a hurry. Today, the man the Church remembers as its writer, and why his sign is a lion.
screen: `NO MANGER, NO ANGELS.` → `A SHOUT FROM THE WILDERNESS.` → `THE GOSPEL IN A HURRY.`

segments.voice: Who was Mark? The Gospel itself never says. Tradition fills in the name. An early bishop, Papias, wrote that Mark had been Peter's interpreter, and set down what Peter remembered of the Lord's words and deeds. Tradition also links him with the John Mark of the Acts of the Apostles, whose mother's house in Jerusalem was a place where the believers gathered, and who set out with Paul and Barnabas, then turned back partway. Paul refused to take him on the next journey, and Paul and Barnabas split over it. Yet in a later letter Paul asks for Mark to be brought to him, because he is useful. A young man who failed once, and was trusted again. Some readers even wonder whether the young man in Mark's own Gospel, who runs off naked from Gethsemane when Jesus is arrested, is the writer quietly signing his work. Nobody can know. Now the lion. Christians long ago matched the four Gospel writers with the four living creatures in Ezekiel and Revelation: a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. Saint Jerome gave Mark the lion, because his Gospel opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness. In the Douay-Rheims: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Venice later took Mark as its patron, and his winged lion still stands over the city. A short Gospel, a loud beginning, and a writer who was given a second chance.
screen: `THE GOSPEL NEVER NAMES ITS WRITER.` · `PETER'S INTERPRETER, TRADITION SAYS.` · `JOHN MARK: FAILED ONCE, TRUSTED AGAIN.` · `A LION FOR A ROARING VOICE.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one chapter of Mark. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or an app nearby, open to Mark, chapter one. If not, just plan when you'll do it today. Chapter one is a short read. As you read, notice the pace. Jesus is always on the move: the river, the desert, the lake, a house full of people, a lonely place before dawn. Let the speed pull you along. If you pray, you can ask to hear it as if for the first time. If you don't, simply read it as a story. The bell holds the time.
Mark. The evangelist the Church names as writer of the Gospel that opens with a voice in the desert, marked by the lion.
Your line: the lion. Today, read Mark chapter one, and see how many places Jesus goes before it ends. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist on 25 April, reading from his Gospel at Mass; in Venice, where tradition says his relics rest, his day is a great civic and church feast.

Claims rule: no dates, counts of chapters or verses, or claims about the Gospel's age spoken. 'Mark's chapters are short; one fits in a coffee break' is a general description; confirm or cut. The carry invites counting places Jesus goes; it is a reading activity, not a claim.

Mark 14:51–52 young man as the author: given as 'some readers wonder' and 'nobody can know'.
Lion for Mark: assigned by Jerome (Irenaeus had a different pairing). Script says 'Saint Jerome gave Mark the lion'; confirm. 'Christians long ago matched' is a vague time claim.
Venice: relics and the winged lion; given as later patronage. Confirm.
